utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before the witness makes a declaration, let me just say that, Mr. Tapuskovic, in relation to the experts that you propose to bring to testify, you, of course, have to abide by the requirement for 30 days' notice. And, of course the Trial Chamber will also need time to assess the report and the Prosecution response. So this is going to require a minimum of one week per report. The Defence should therefore aim to file its notification no later than the 13th of July. The 30 days from that would take us to the 13th of August, and if that is so, then, the experts would be ready to testify the last week of the sitting, which is the 20th of August. So I just ask you to bear that in mind. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. But I have to inform you first that we are assisted today by Marko Momcilovic, an assistant in our team. He is actually a language assistant enabling us to communicate with the witness if that should be required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks for telling us and we are glad to have him. Please commence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon. I appear as Defence counsel for the accused, Dragomir Milosevic, as you are already aware. You don't need more details. We have been in touch over the past few days in proofing that took several hours. Could you now please introduce yourself to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: My name is Andrei Demurenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Chamber your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I was born on the 28th of April, 1955.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell the Judges about your educational background and your specialised training, just an outline.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: With pleasure. After graduating from high school, I enrolled in an army school, in Moscow, following a four-year course, and after several years of command duty in the army, I went to the Frunze Academy, Military Academy. I also attended an American US staff college. I have a science degree and I am an a Ph.D., actually, and I'm one of the military experts on a US NATO commission. My Ph.D. Is in military science.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Judges, as a military man, before you became a member of the UN mission to Bosnia whether you served in another military mission elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No, I only served in the Soviet army and, after that, in the army of the Russian Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you then tell us briefly about your service in the armed forces of the Russian Federation, what duties did you discharge there, what posts did you occupy?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I am a general army commander, that is, a commander that can exert command duty over all branches of service. I was platoon commander, company commander, battalion commander. I was Chief of Staff in a regiment. Then over two and a half years I commanded a regiment in the Far East on the Chinese border. Following that, I was a senior officer in the operations headquarters of the armed services of the Russian Federation, in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges if you are specialised or have particular knowledge about a certain kind of weapon?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Naturally I am familiar with the entire arsenal that was at the disposal of the units that I just enumerated in my previous answer. All the infantry weaponry, all the artillery, including 155-millimetre Howitzers and machine-guns of all calibres, 62 -- sorry, 60, 82, 120-millimetres, tanks, APCs, the entire arsenal briefly that the Russian army had at the tactical level, that is, the level of division. I'm perfectly familiar with all these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges whether that weaponry used by the Russian Federation was similar to the arsenal used by the former Yugoslav peoples army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Without a doubt. As we well know, the Yugoslavia army used Soviet-produced weaponry, delivered by the Soviet Union with the exception of certain infantry weapons. All that was used in the battlefields of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I mean the warring parties, of course, was perfectly familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, when you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, what rank did you hold in the Russian army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I was a colonel when I arrived -- I'm sorry, the brief answer is I was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you arrive in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a member of the UN mission?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: It was in the first decade of January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges when you served there in the UNPROFOR what were your duties? What was your job in that context?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I was Chief of Staff for the Sarajevo Sector. That was the name of my post. As you know, the Chief of Staff is the first deputy of the commander in any army, practically I was the first deputy commander for the Sarajevo Sector. My responsibilities included practically the same duties as those of the commander, decision taking, issuing orders, verifying the execution of orders and tasks issued by the commanding staff of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While we are at -- on your background, just tell us how long did you stay in Sector Sarajevo in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Practically one year, from January until almost the end of December. Almost an entire year. December 1995, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you: When did you finish your military career?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I retired from the Russian army in December 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges what that means. What is your current occupation? Does it mean that you are retired?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Precisely. I retired from the army and I am now in the status of reserve colonel. I'm still on the mobilisation list in the Russian Federation in case of mobilisation, but I'm now a civilian and I work as director of a shipping wharf.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is my duty to ask you this: How many years did you serve in the army, briefly?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Well, very briefly, around 26 years, from 1972 to 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you retired for a particular reason? Why did you withdraw from the army; could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: It is a bit personal rather than for professional reasons. Everything was fine as far as my professional service was concerned, but one reason that convinced me it was time to retire was this: Throughout my career, I was a successful officer with three degrees in military science. I was promoted very quickly through the ranks. However, in the General Staff I could not be promoted to general although it was only one step away for one simple reason. Conservative views prevail in the Russian army to such an extent that a person who graduated from an American Military Academy and could potentially propagate American views absolutely cannot receive the rank of general, and that is why I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Demurenko. I think that will suffice in terms of your background. And it will suffice for the further line of my questioning. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, before you go into the examination-in-chief, I would like, if you could assist us in establishing the witness's expertise. I think the witness said that he was an expert in military science, but I would be interested in knowing which field of military science.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, I, as Defence counsel did not call this witness as an expert, but I appreciate your question and I will ask it of the witness. That is why I tried to elicit his background in the army. But I can ask it directly as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you know, for instance, about artillery weapons? Was it in any way related to your activities?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you meant the part of the witness's answer when he said he had a Ph.D., I can ask him in what field he has a Ph.D. He said military science.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Demurenko, could you please try to answer Judge Harhoff's question. What is the exact field of your Ph.D.?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Certainly. I have a master of arts degree or a master of -- or a BS in political science. I was the first in Russia who defended a thesis on the topic of use of armed forces in peace keeping operations, and I can also tell you about my knowledge concerning artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. I was just interested in finding out if you had any particular expertise or knowledge about some of the things that you will be questioned about. But there's no need to go further into this, and I kindly ask Mr. Tapuskovic to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, please, quickly, Witness, you said that you left the army because a promotion would be almost impossible because you had been to a Military Academy in the States. If that is the tradition in the army of your country, not to promote anyone who has been to a US Military Academy, I would like to know who sent you there to study and why you accepted to actually go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer with pleasure. During the so-called Perestroika time-period afterwards, Russia started establishing very actively international relations and at the time the two presidents agreed at the highest level to have exchange of scholars, specialists in order to have good scientific cooperation in the field. I turned out to be the first and the last officer who, in the whole history of Russia over the past several hundred years was admitted to a US staff college, completed it successfully and then returned back to -- hoping and I returned with gratitude, feeling great gratitude to the United States, hoping that I would be able to use what I had learned and experienced in the US. Unfortunately, the relations between the two countries changed for the worse. The mentality of Russian generals in the Ministry of Defence did not keep up with the democratic changes in the country. So the idea was a very good one, but its implementation unfortunately, the situation was not ripe for its implementation. I don't know, perhaps in 10 or 12 years the Russian army will be prepared to nurture its generals in the western countries. At the time there were not ready to do that in my case. I was told this personally by a very high military official in the Russian Federation. Unfortunately, I cannot tell you his name right now, but he told me this personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, let us now go into the substance. Let me ask you this first. While you served in Bosnia-Herzegovina in your position there from January to October 1995, did you ever get to meet General Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Until December. I served until December.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're quite right. So please tell me, during one year that you were there, did you ever meet General Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No, we did not meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said earlier that you were Chief of Staff of Sector Sarajevo. Thus, I'd like to show the UNPROFOR map to you, 2829. Mr. Demurenko, could you please show us the building or, rather, the location where your staff was headquartered in Sarajevo Sector. If you can circle that location, please, and put a letter S there.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the area of responsibility, the area that you had under your control, the area for which you were responsible. What did that encompass? Which parts of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of Sarajevo Sector included the area shown on the map and even broader than that. I can tell you, looking at the map that everything that was inside the confrontation lines, that is to say, the city of Sarajevo itself, plus the outlying area, extending 10 to 15, up to 20 kilometres, all of that was included in our area of responsibility, and I was a Chief of Staff or the first deputy of the commander for Sector Sarajevo, and naturally all of that territory was included in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have shown this map to you previously, and I, at the time, did not make any suggestions to you. Is that correct? I wish to ask you this. You see that there is a red line here and a yellow line. Do you understand what they stand for?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Naturally. This is the front end of defence or the forward end of defence, as we call it in the military, of the two warring sides. The yellow line is the BiH army line, and the red line is that of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could it be said that the entire territory inside the yellow line was under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Undoubtedly, yes. Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean -- I do not wish to go into details and give names for each of these locations but does this mean that each location inside this line was under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that, once again, and I can give you the location names, Mojmilo, Zuc, Grbavica, everything lying within the yellow line was under the control of the BH army, and I personally went to inspect this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Grbavica. Who had Grbavica under their control? Under whose control was Grbavica? You mentioned Grbavica as well, but please look at the lines. Are you sure that Grbavica was under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No, I wasn't accurate enough when it comes to the names of locations. I practically know this map by heart. What I wanted to say is that everything shown on the map, all of these names that can be seen on the map, was something that was within my area of responsibility. I didn't claim that Grbavica was under the control of the BH army. What I'm say something that everything inside the yellow line was under the control of the BH army and everything shown on this map was within the area of responsibility of my forces, of the UN Sarajevo Sector. The reason why I mentioned Grbavica is that there was a Russian Battalion stationed there. They belonged to the UN forces and, naturally, I visited them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tender this map marked as it is now into evidence as Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D285, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, you have already told the Judges that you came to Bosnia and Herzegovina in January of 1995. Could you please tell the Chamber how it was at the time when you arrived, what happened during the first few months of your stay. Would you be able to describe it to the Judge, please? Naturally, I ask you to focus on what you personally observed first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: It was winter time, and it turned to be quite a peculiar period of time in Sarajevo, because regardless of the fact that there was cease-fire in force, from time to time several times a day and particularly at night, one could hear shots fired from infantry weapons. If you are interested in the daily life in the city, then I can tell you that I was somewhat surprised by the slow, even-paced life of the citizens in the city. Naturally, they were anxious because of the fact that the town was under siege, but they also had a bit of ambivalent attitude, blunted attitude toward life. Let me give you an example. There was a French Battalion within the UN contingent and they went out to clean the streets. The residents refused to clean trash and rubbish from the streets and the French soldiers went out to do it for them. So this is just an example of people from the outside doing what the local residents should be doing. As for the military activity, there was practically none during winter time. The activity, if I can call it, in quotation marks, boiled down to sporadic shooting and occasional explosion. This wouldn't happen more frequently than once or twice a week. The information arriving from military monitors and UN observation posts indicated that those explosions were a result of mortar shells, but the majority of them were caused by improvised devices, which were manufactured by warring sides in an amateur way. And for us, officers of modern armies, that would be ridiculous had it not caused bloodshed and tears. They would, for example, take a barrel, fill it up with gas or with petrol and then they would use a simple cloth to -- simple rag to close it off and then they would detonate it, detonate the fuse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- with matches and then they would roll it to the side held by the enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not fond of this narrative approach. I don't know where this is going to end. Put a specific question to the witness so we can have a specific answer. You speak of they detonating. Who is "they," Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was simply speaking about this pseudo military activity of these handmade devices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who would be -- who are the persons who would be carrying out those actions? Would it be members of the ABiH or the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our information pointed to the fact that both sides resorted to this, not very often. As I told you, this was once a week, but we heard these explosions. We registered them and they were caused by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Demurenko, Your Honour, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you said just now that the town was under siege and then also describe your area of responsibility, the area that was under your control, if we were to look at this map and at the red line, you mentioned Grbavica earlier. But how about Nedzarici? Can you please explain what you meant by mentioning these locations and by mentioning the siege. Who was under siege in that territory that you had under your control?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to give you specific names of settlements and details about the activity there, because I'm not sure that I could give you an accurate picture of what happened 12 years ago. But as for the map, let me repeat once again. The army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was inside. They defended the forward defence lines which are the positions marked with yellow. In addition to the forward defence lines there were also units of the BH army that were in reserve. They were either taking rest or they were rotating and going to the forward defence lines. As for the red lines, those were the forward defence lines of the army of Republika Srpska. There is nothing else to add to this. I would rather not use the names of geographic locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, but if we were to look at the location where the Russian Battalion was stationed, which was Grbavica, can you tell us about its geographic position or can you tell us something about Nedzarici. You know very well where Nedzarici is located. What was their geographic position?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I apologise, I did not receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, you know where this area of Sarajevo is located, Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Russian Battalion was not in Nedzarici. It was in Grbavica. The Russian Battalion was station -- was billeted in the former barracks of the Yugoslavia peoples army or something resembling it. I'm not quite familiar with the history of that building. It was just a typical -- those were typical premises for billeting, and around it they had observation posts and areas that they patrolled. That's all that I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Demurenko. We've been speaking Russian over the past few days and I seem to have forgotten my native language. What I asked you had to do with the location of Grbavica, where the Russian Battalion was stationed. Do you remember what two features, geographic features were important when it comes to Grbavica? Or perhaps if you don't remember, we can drop the subject.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: My only memory about the location of the Russian Battalion in Grbavica was that it was particularly disadvantageous, extremely unfavourable. I don't know who decided to choose that location, but it was a very unfortunate choice, because from the side of the Sarajevo, in fact from both sides there were dominating hills overlooking the headquarters of the battalion, which put the soldiers of the Russian Battalion in an unfavourable position vis-a-vis those who were shooting, including those from the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, if we could complete your story about the initial period. How would you describe those first months in terms of what you have seen, and how long would you say that initial period lasted?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Taking into account the comment of the Honourable Judge, I will try to refrain from a narrative and emotional description. It was a period of stagnant confrontation. It was not a military confrontation in the standard sense of the word. There was standard shooting -- sporadic shooting without particular targets or missions. Before April, none of the sides undertook any tactical movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now you mention April. How far into April did this stretch?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Beginning with the first week of April, intensity increasing day by day, the activity of both sides was on the rise, in terms of intensity of shooting, movement of troops along the forward line, in terms of the fierceness of exchanges of fire. If we were to draw a chart, it would be a steadily rising line, peaking in June. At any rate, the military activity of the warring parties steadily increased, beginning with April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Demurenko, did something unusual happen in May, and, if so, could you describe it to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Apart from the intensified activity of the warring parties and the air-strike and rocket strikes against Serbian targets, I don't seem to recall anything much. My most vivid memory from that period was from June, when, as a result of an ABH attack, a Russian observation post was occupied and it was my task to take it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now you mention this, could you describe it in greater detail. Whose operation was that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Speaking in military lingo, it's at the tactical level. An operation begins with the operational level. It was a battle. The local attack of the BH army along a southward direction, starting approximately from their forward line as shown on the map, towards the location occupied by the Russian platoon, the distance was three kilometres and it was exposed to fire from both sides and for reasons we could not understand, a company strength unit around 50, 60 men strong unit of the BH army attacked, crossed that area, they overcame, overran a platoon strong unit of the UN from the Russian contingent creating an incident, as a result of which I had to take urgent measures to solve this problem. The methods were standard. On one hand, one had to ensure the support of the UNPROFOR command and commission the necessary number of APCs to get to the forward line under fire. Then, I had to resolve with the leadership, at least of the 1st corps of the BH army and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps on the Serb side, to cease-fire so that I could take back my soldiers without any casualties, and what is remarkable is that I succeeded. After certain telephone calls among the leadership, they agreed to cease-fire for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what will be the relevance of this evidence of the ABiH occupying a Russian observation post and the post being retaken by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he cited an example and he first mentioned that offensive and the combat operations that started in June. I would just like to go through a few more questions before I take him back to what happened in June and July. He described one operation and then we shall see what actually happened, who initiated the combat in June and July and I don't want to suggest any answer to the witness, but the idea of the Defence is to show what the combat operations looked like, especially in May, June, July, August, and through to the end of the conflict. Now, for what reason, I have explained already more than once. It is our case that many things depended on operations initiated by the BH army and that is why I want to take the witness back to the incident which I believe is very important as a part of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon Mr. President. For what it's worth the Prosecution has no objection for this background information to come in, rather than I'm more hesitant to allow the Defence to kind of again, argue his case almost in a closing argument in front of the witness. So the Prosecution has no objections to this background information to be led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful to you for that, but it's the Chamber that will decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will not allow any more evidence on this matter to be given. The Chamber does not consider the evidence to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, am I allowed to ask him at all what happened in June and July 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As long as it is relevant, yes. As long as it is relevant. We have ruled that evidence about the taking of the Russian observation post by the ABiH and its retaking by the witness is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you cited this example and we now have to abide by the ruling of the Chamber, no contest. What else happened in June and July? You told us about one operation. But what about the other combat activities that escalated in June, as you said?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Truth to tell, there was no other activity apart from the activities of the warring parties in the period of June, July and August. The activity of the warring parties intensified steadily, but they were static in nature. There were no major movements of troops. It was trench war mainly. At that moment it was increasingly important, in view of the situation to increasingly use artillery weapons that was somehow taken from heavy weaponry depots. And that, to a lesser or greater degree, contributed to increased activities and increased casualties in that period. It was civil war, trench war. Apart from that, I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, Colonel. What do you mean by civil war? That was the translation. But I didn't understand the meaning of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand a civil war to mean exactly what it is defined as in the dictionary. There was no outside attack on Yugoslavia. Warring sides that used to be citizens of one and the same country started fighting each other, and these groups differed in ethnicity and confession. On the Bosnian side, I saw not only one religion, and among the Serbs as well I saw members of different confessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You certainly mean -- or do you mean fighting by combatants in the military sense of that word -- in the legal sense of that word? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You just said something about casualties. Did you tour the area at the time of the conflict, at the time of fierce fighting, and what kind of casualties are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: In the course of military operations and sporadic exchanges of fire, I saw both dead and wounded. Actually, I didn't see them in the street, in the battlefield. I didn't run across them in the street because my duties were mainly at the headquarters, but I saw them in field hospitals and other locations on the forward defence lines. A wounded soldier, a civilian is usually taken to the hospital at the defence line. I saw wounded on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you visit hospitals on both sides?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I did not go on purpose to visit hospitals, but occasionally I was forced to go there. For example, there was a small French hospital was in the UNPROFOR forces and they provided emergency assistance to the wounded soldiers of the BH army before turning them over to Sarajevo hospitals, and on those occasions, and on those occasions -- on one of those cases I saw a surgeon operate on a BH army soldier. Occasionally I would visit hospitals, not because I wanted to visit a wounded, but during my tours -- during one of my tours, I saw a Serb being carried on a stretcher and I couldn't tell you whether he was a resident of a local village or what. I just saw that he was wounded, and they -- that he was wounded and that he was carried away. But I couldn't tell you whether he was a civilian or a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you visit a hospital in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was just telling you about. That was the case I just told you about. As we were passing by Lukavica, I saw a wounded man being taken to the Lukavica hospital, and after seeing that, I entered the hospital and I was able to see for myself that in the hospital they provided treatment, medical assistance, to this wounded Serb. That's what I saw with my own eyes. I saw similar cases on the Bosnian side. I saw both wounded and dead being taken to medical institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question concerning that. When you entered that hospital and when you saw that wounded man, were there any other wounded persons in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: If you're referring to the hospital in Lukavica, then, yes, there were other wounded people there. I saw them in beds. And if you're referring to the French hospital, which was located near my headquarters, then I can tell you that I saw one soldier being operated on. However, based on reports and briefings I know that there were many similar cases. This was just a typical case of assistance to one of the wounded BH soldiers. That was a typical case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you are familiar with the event which took place on the 28th of August, 1995. It is usually referred to as Markale 2. Have you heard of this event?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm quite familiar with that. I personally participated in investigating the incident. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, first of all, I'd like to ask you about something that preceded that incident. On that day, on the 28th of August, 1995, when were you informed about that event?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: The operations centre, the operations centre which was located in our headquarters was on line and gathering information about the activity of the warring sides. Several minutes after the Markale incident, observation posts were informed about that. The information arrived at the operations centre, a standard type of report was prepared there, and through -- or, rather, within a 30-minute period of time, it was already on the table of the sector commander, Chief of Staff and other deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember anything about the time. What were you told about when that had happened? What did they tell you? Approximately, naturally.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: This was not a verbal report. As I told you, we had a written report, hard copy report on the desks. Just after taking a glance at the report, it became clear to me that this was not an ordinary case of shelling, because there was a large number of casualties. A figure of several tens of casualties was mentioned. This number was such that it required immediate action.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While you were there at the headquarters, did you have to do something after receiving this kind of information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: In accordance with my duties, my official duties, my level was such that it did not require me to do anything special. UNPROFOR, just like other peace keeping forces, UNPROFOR forces acted in accordance with the standard operating procedures that I was quite familiar with, due to my American schooling. Based on standard operating procedures, after any incident causing casualties, units or brigades begin initial investigation. Thus, I wasn't duty-bound to jump from my chair and run into town to see what had happened. I knew that standard operating procedures were already in place, steps were already taken at the time when I received the written report on my desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell Their Honours when you arrived at the site, what time it was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Waespi is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, just an observation. I don't think the witness said that he went to the site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you go to the site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I didn't jump immediately and run to the site because I was the Chief of Staff. However, I did go to the site two hours later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you went to the site of the incident. Did you do anything yourself at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes. Upon arriving there, I observed the crater of the impact. I saw that the experts were there working at the site. I saw blood on the pavement, on the street. I made an initial observation of the causes -- or, rather, consequences of this attack, of this shell landing there. Following that, I gave instructions to the UNPROFOR members working at the site, and then I went back to the headquarters in order to prepare appropriate orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Judges whether upon your return back to the headquarters you learned anything else about the event itself?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I did learn the following, something that actually shocked me. Upon my return to the headquarters, I learned that the spokesperson of UNPROFOR in Bosnia and Herzegovina who I think was a British lieutenant-colonel, organised speedily a press conference where he said something that was unacceptable. Actually illegal. The spokesman said that this was just another example of an atrocity and a crime committed by Serbian army and that they need to be punished and condemned as the enemies of humanity. This was completely groundless. There were absolutely no grounds for him to state something like, because nobody could say something like that before the investigation was concluded. What he did was actually an act of provocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So how much time elapsed from the event until you heard that this was stated? How much time elapsed between that and your return to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I understood your question. As I have told you, I went to the site two hours after it had taken place. I spent there some 30 minutes working. It took me another 30 minutes to arrive back at the headquarters, and upon my arrival there, I heard that there had been this statement made, which is to say that the statement was made two to two and a half hours after the incident. This man took it upon himself to state something that he had no right to state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, did additional information arrive in the course of the day, be it officially or unofficially?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: It was not my duty to collect official information. However, the required documents were on my desk, were put on my desk. Namely, those were the results of this initial investigation. What kind of documents were those? Those were two reports, if I can remember well. The first one was a report made by a Dutch officer who was a ballistics trajectory expert. The second report was produced by a ballistic expert who was either a Croat or an expert from Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is something that you can easily verify if you look in the records. Something very simple was stated there. They established the angle of approach, of descent at the time the shell reached the surface. It was a very important document, which allowed us to proceed with the investigation, to go further with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, under the circumstances, upon receiving these two reports, did you speak to anyone who was your superior? At the time who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: At the time General Bachelet was my commander. He replaced General Gobillard there, some month and a half earlier. I went to see him with a briefing, where I proposed to head myself an investigation group, because it was absolutely inappropriate not to do anything similar, given what a tragic event had taken place, and he gave me his consent. He okayed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I proceeded to investigate, to organise an investigation. I had to gather a working group of experts who were to assist me in my work. I was to collect all existing documents, including those reports that I have mentioned. The investigation itself -- or, rather, the work of the investigation itself was not a complicated one. This is something that had been done many times in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. I'd like to ask you, Witness, whether it was normal procedure for a person in your position to propose that you yourself would head an investigation into this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can give you my answer. It was not a typical, standard procedure. In each sectors there were groups that normally undertook such investigation. However, given the number of casualties -- and their number increased hour by hour. Initially we were told a couple of dozen casualties and then within an hour the numbers grew to 30 dead and 70 wounded and then within the next hour that in turn increased to 50 and 80, respectively. At the end the figure quoted was 120. Given the consequences, I thought that it required a non-standard approach, and I took it upon myself to head this investigation. It is true normally that such investigations are typically headed by a captain or a major, not by a colonel. It is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said that after the event the UNPROFOR spokesperson, a British officer, made a statement which, according to you, was illegal. Given your position, you were head of staff, I would like to know if you had punished this British officer or if somebody within the chain of command had taken measures against this person to show that he had actually committed a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, he was not my subordinate. I need to explain this to you. There were two staffs in Sarajevo. There was a large staff which was the UNPROFOR command for the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then there was also Sector Sarajevo, which represented only a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was Chief of Staff of Sarajevo Sector, and this spokesman worked for the entire UNPROFOR command for Bosnia and Herzegovina. His superior was General Rupert Smith; therefore, I was not able to punish somebody who was not my subordinate. As for him being punished at all, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you don't know if he was ever punished, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about that, correct. Perhaps he was promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, I wanted to use a different approach, but given what you said about seeing two reports on that day which prompted you to take certain measures, as you described to us, I would now like to show something else. I would like you to focus on this now. I will show you a document dated on that day which was sent to Mr. Kofi Annan. Same date document. This is Exhibit D00-D10 [As translated].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please bring it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now and have a look at the document when we return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, you will now see a document, D00-10. If you please, would you like at page 1 first of the English version, because you speak English. It's a document from August 1995. Look at the heading to see who is sending this document, the source of this document, which officer. Towards the top, you see "from," and then the name of the person. It says August 1995 and then in the next line it's "from."

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-General Janvier. That was the Force Commander?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: The Force Commander of the UNPROFOR for the entire Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now see who the recipient is, who is it addressed to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Certainly. Kofi Annan, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at page 2 of this document, English version, which is page 3 in B/C/S; in fact, 4. Further -- or, rather, earlier you saw it was from August and now you see the exact date. What is that date? Top of the page.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: 29 August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look more carefully? Maybe we should scroll down a bit. I'm not going to suggest the answer to you. But could we lower the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You know, this is document I don't object to leading the witness to a passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document from 28th August 1995. Do you agree? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have to answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, as far as I could see the document was actually dated the 29th of August, at least the English version. There was a date on the top of the -- on the right side of the top of the page which I thought said 29th of August. There you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, this document is dated 28th and it refers to the 28th of August. You see it in the heading. It's an UNPROFOR report for the 28th of August, and we are now going to look at the page that I want to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not contested it is a report dated 28th of August addressed to Kofi Annan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's see whether Mr. Waespi can shed light on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I don't want to testify but this appears to be a standard daily situation report which covers the whole, as you see at the front page, cover page, the whole of the 28th August, from the first minute to 23.59, and it was faxed, it appears to me, on the 29th of August, 1995 at 10.36 to whoever. But maybe the gentleman can tell us, you know, the way these reports were drafted, these sitreps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You seem to be quite knowledgeable yourself, Mr. Waespi, in military matters. Witness, can you shed some light on this? How are we to read it? Are we to read it in the way Mr. Waespi just suggested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Strictly speaking, this is a standard report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are concerned with the date. It's the date. We know it's a standard report, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Why does it have the 29th of August, as Judge Harhoff pointed out, at the very top?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see also the 29th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you explain it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I cannot explain it, because in order to explain that I would have to know the entire procedure of drafting. There are types of reports that cover the previous day, but they are dated on the date of sending, which is perfectly normal, especially if one was sending a report on line to the Secretary-General. But speaking specifically of the document in front of me, I can say nothing in particular, apart from the fact that it refers to Sarajevo saying that a certain number of shells, five shells fell on the centre of Sarajevo, causing casualties, including more than 30 dead. I cannot add anything to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We note the -- the distinction, the discrepancy, if indeed it is a discrepancy, and we will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will refrain from giving my own interpretation because there is no reason for me to do so, but I would like the witness to see now the second page of this report concerning Sarajevo. In the B/C/S version it will be page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, could you please look at page 2, UNPROFOR, paragraph 1, Sector Sarajevo. That's English page 2. Please pay attention to the beginning of this sentence, which begins with: "At 11.10." Could you read this aloud, slowly?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It says here that the mortar shells that impacted, at least one of them, and the coordinates are indicated, killed over 30 persons and injured more than 80. This mortar shell was assessed to be fired from 170 degrees and the investigation showed that the distance to the firing point is still to be determined. The definition of firing positions for mortar rounds is very difficult, as it is impossible to determine the level of charge used to fire the projectiles. Follow descriptions of mortar shells that were fired by different warring factions, et cetera. Briefly what is described here is the difficulty of determining the fire points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, I have to come back to this later, but now I'm asking you, if this report had reached the headquarters of your command at the same time as those other two reports, would you have still asked General Bachelet to take any steps, in view of what had already been stated at the press conference?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Well, my reply would have to be as follows: If the data available, if the standard data was not sufficient, namely, that there was an attack and there were casualties but the perpetrator could not be determined yet, and if there had been no statements, no public statements on the subject, then I would not have been required to take any further steps to investigate personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show the witness another report, also for the 28th of August, Prosecution Exhibit P85.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you see in this handwritten text the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. The 28th, 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since this is not in dispute and this is a Prosecution Exhibit, the document was issued by Colonel Konings. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Look at point 2 of this report. Could you please read it. Aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Let me tell you frankly, I can tell you bits and pieces, because I cannot read the whole of it. It's not legible enough. Obviously, it speaks of an artillery attack, a shelling attack. It says it is impossible to determine the fire point with accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Demurenko, it is my fault. I wasn't precise enough. Read the second point. It's very brief. Just one sentence. It begins with: "The bearings ..."

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I cannot make out one word. Then it says -- oh, it's perfect now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Assuming the B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Estimated angle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When counsel is on his feet, witness, you must stop speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: There is a B/C/S version and which is more legible because it is a translation, and perhaps that's helpful for the witness as well, although the last second he said he can read it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is now zoomed in. Make you can read it out now, para 2.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I will, in Russian. It says: "The bearings in combination the estimated angle of impact could give no evidence on the origin of fire ... Briefly, the conclusion is that it was impossible to identify the perpetrator of this attack with any accuracy at the current moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, if on the 28th of August, as Chief of Staff, you had had this report by Lieutenant-Colonel Konings, would you have still gone to General Bachelet to ask for permission to undertake any steps as Chief of Staff personally?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I have to say this once again. This is perfectly natural. It would have been very odd indeed if in wartime everybody knew everything immediately. Under the circumstances a constant exchange of fire, it is difficult to establish the truth. What is critical in determining the perpetrator of an attack, one has to have in mind two things that happened, two major things that happened. First of all, the public statement that was made and shouldn't have been made by the spokesman of the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, please. My question was very brief after you have read this. If you had had this report in front of you, as should have been the case, would you have gone to General Bachelet to ask for anything?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No, I would not have approached him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness another document dated 29 August, DD117. Your Honours, I ask for your leave to read this in B/C/S to save time. This will help us go through this document more quickly and will help me focus the witness on what is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the length?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness could confirm the date and confirm the identity of the signatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see the 29th of August, Lieutenant-Colonel Konings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two very brief paragraphs that I would like to read to the witness and they are not in dispute. This document entirely is not in dispute because it has been admitted already, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, here at the beginning this report is related to the report of the UNMO patrol dated 28th August 1995, paragraph 2, on the following page, under number 4 AA says: "At the time when five impacts occurred, Military Observers of the UN from the CC team on observation posts did not see or hear the shells fired either from the territory of the Bosnian army or the territory of the Bosnian Serbs." And then under point 3 it says: "All facts from the previous reports remain unchanged and valid." If you had known about this report on the 29th, would you have continued any activities related to the problem that was the subject of that announcement or that communique made the previous day? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: In that context the answer would be yes, because this report shows, again, the amount of confusion and contradiction involved in various reports from various sources and it shows how wrong the spokesman was to take it upon himself to make that announcement the way he did. So my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. What did you do after all. You talked to General Bachelet. And what did you do afterwards?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I gathered a group of experts. Those were my closest aides. I set a task, I defined the task, namely, to make ballistic calculations in order to either confirm or deny the information given by the first expert on the angle of impact of the shell upon the surface. Second, to calculate the angle of the shell, to show it on the map, to, rather, draw the line of descent on the map. Further, the investigation was supposed to include personal inspection of all possible fire positions of that particular shell, including photo documentation of those locations. The task was defined. On the following day we started implementing it. The experts used charts or tables, firing tables for 120-millimetre mortars. They also prepared drawings of the angle of descent, and then on the following day we made -- we made a site visit where I made photographs, which became part of the investigation file. That's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you finish your task? When did you finish your work with the expert team? You started working on the following day, and when did you conclude your work?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: We worked for three days, on the 29th, 30th and 31st. On the 1st I had the results of investigation together with appropriate conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do then? Did you communicate this to your superiors? Did you try to do anything about this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes. I prepared appropriate material. I wanted to report in the standard procedure. I wanted to brief the commander on the results of the investigation. However, I had an encounter with his assistant who was a Canadian officer, and this changed my mind about that. When I came with the results of the investigation and I showed the conclusions to the assistant and the assistant realised that our conclusions differed from those prepared by the public and UNPROFOR spokesperson, this Canadian officer told me, "There will be no publishing of your report, it will be impossible to publish it, announce it, or to give this report to the commander." When I heard this, I took my report and the photographs and I left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Colonel, what exactly did your report conclude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was just one conclusion. The result of the investigation indicated that the Serbs could not have fired the shell in that incident. The Serbs did not do it. Rather, the army of Republika Srpska did not do it. I have arguments to support this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you only find a negative? Were you able to conclude who -- who did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was very important to maintain the principle of impartiality of an UNPROFOR officer. I set a task for myself to expose the lies stated by the spokesperson about Serbs being the aggressors in that particular incident. It was not my task to show who fired that shell. This is a very important principle, and I can explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something that follows from what you just said. Now that we have touched upon this issue of who had done it. Mr. Demurenko, did anyone say anything two hours or several hours after the incident? Did somebody say anything about the truth being established, or, rather, would you have done the same had somebody asked you to do it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I would have used all my professional efforts. I would have aimed all my professional efforts at establishing the truth, regardless of whether the truth suited somebody or not. I would like to draw your attention to the fact that it is the duty of an UNPROFOR officer to act without any bias and not state lies to the public. Had the spokesperson stated that it was done by the Bosnian side, I would have still set the same task to myself, namely to establish the truth, to expose the lie. Had somebody made a rumour that this was caused by an American missile, I would have still acted the same, because all lies need to be exposed. Now, as to establishing who had actually done it, that would be the next step.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko -- or, rather, Your Honour Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that there were lies about Serb aggressions or Bosnian aggressions or US aggressions in your example. Where did you get the presumption from that there were lies about who did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to reiterate that I was wasn't trying to prove anybody's guilt in this. All I was trying to do was to show that UNPROFOR was a professional, non-political force of the United Nations. The task of UNPROFOR is to be as objective as possible. The person who claimed that the Serbs were guilty in this incident had no grounds to do that, had no results of an investigation ready yet. Therefore, this should not have been announced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Any investigation, including your own investigation, I assume would have been made with the purpose of establishing where the missile was fired from, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was supposed to be the second step. The first step was what was announced and then the second step should have been to announce the perpetrator. I was not allowed to continue with my investigation, and it is difficult for me to say why I wasn't allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I interpret your reference to the result of your first investigation to imply that the BiH would have fired those missiles, because if the result of the first investigation you made was that it could not have been the Serbs, then the obvious conclusion to be drawn from that fact have been that it would then have been the Bosnian army who had fired the shell. Would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wouldn't want to follow that line of thought as to the second step of the investigation. I have my point of view based on certain evidence, and my point of view is that there was no shelling attack. This was a terrorist attack. This was something that was done within Sarajevo. It was a provocation. However, right now, I don't have in my hands either any arguments or evidence to support this. However, there are some indicators of what I'm claiming, and I found indicators of that while I was in Sarajevo. However, we're running ahead of ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Meaning what? When you say "running ahead of ourselves," does that mean that later on in the testimony you will be telling us about those indicators. You will be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, at last the trial is becoming interesting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can swear to you that I did not discuss this topic with the witness at all. It is my duty to explain this to you. I wanted to first conclude his evidence, and then I thought that it would be up to you to evaluate his evidence. Naturally I realise that the Judges have every right to intervene at any moment, but let us try first to conclude with the evidence of this witness and then turn to the issues mentioned just now by the witness. This is quite a surprise for me as well. Now, by your leave, Your Honour Robinson, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to General Bachelet, you went to his office and you were told what you told us about. What did you do in that situation? Could you please explain that to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, we are now back to the 28th of August in the evening, because the way I understand it -- the evidence on the 1st, when the gentleman wanted to see General Bachelet, he was kind of stopped by the military assistant. I just want to know which encounter with General Bachelet are we talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It involves following. On the 28th, in the evening, I addressed General Bachelet directly, suggesting to him that I had an investigation group because the incident was quite a significant one. It wasn't just any old incident. On the 28th, in the evening, he consented to this. He said that it was all right for me to head this investigation group. Now, the question put to me by Mr. Tapuskovic refers to the events on the 1st, when I was prepared to go see General Bachelet with the results of my investigation. However, his assistant, upon seeing my conclusions in my report, quite clearly said that there was no chance of this report ever reaching General Bachelet and that there was no chance of ever publicising the results of the investigation, so my attempt to reach General Bachelet was not a successful one and I can continue with what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question is actually what followed. What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I had two avenues open to me. The first avenue was to cease any activity and not do anything else in order to promote the investigation. The second avenue was not quite a proper one from the point of view of military ethics and subordination but I had to resort it. Through the liaison officer for public relations, I got in touch with a media company in order to publicise the reports. This liaison officer agreed to have an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which agency conducted an interview with you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Associated Press.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges this: When you were deciding on whether to have the interview or not, what was your dilemma that you had as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he hasn't said -- has he said he a dilemma? He did? Yes. Very well. Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was a dilemma. The first option open to me was not to do anything and just to routinely complete my service. This dilemma still persists with me. It still troubles me. That was probably the first and the last time in my life that I violated the principle of insubordination. I realised that I would get into trouble. My superior, General Bachelet, for him I have sincere admiration, he is a very decent man. I did something to get him into trouble and from the point of view of military subordination, I deserve the punishment. I also got into trouble. General Smith, who was in charge of UNPROFOR for Bosnia and Herzegovina, it wasn't proper to leak this information through inappropriate channels. There was additional problem that concerned me personally. I knew that my chance of surviving in that situation was one to 1.000. I was actually supposed to die there in Sarajevo, because nobody was able to take out to the world that information in a situation where I was surrounded by hostile forces and population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I received the footage of the interview from the Prosecutor's office a few days ago. I think it is necessary for Defence but also for the OTP to show the Defence. It is around 14 minutes long. I believe we should view it in its entirety. The interview was provided in English. We had it translated into B/C/S and it is in e-court. We have turned over the B/C/S translation to the translation service. I believe it would be necessary for us to see the footage so that I can continue my line of questioning, and I believe that the Prosecutor will have some follow-up questions as well. I want to show you the footage by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we will see the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is DD00-4130, the transcript that is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I would like to explain certain details of the investigation conducted by UN experts and has to do with the horrific event that took place a few days ago. As you know, there was a shell that landed in the very centre of town. Over 35 people were killed and more than 80 wounded, as the reports state. As a professional, I cannot agree with the argument put forth by UN experts as to the reasons and the source of the explosion. It is completely unacceptable for me and my colleagues in this area to accept those arguments. That is why I'll try to explain some new information that I have at my disposal. First of all, if you're familiar with the main basic facts, these are as follows: This is the material with the results of the UN experts' report. This copy is in French and contains several very surprising conclusions, including the idea of the place of origin of that shell, meaning that it originated from the Serbian side. This is a sketch depicting the angle under which the shell landed in Marshal Tito street. This is the angle between the ground surface and the angle of descent of the shell. That is it very important. These are copies of the photographs of the street. This is the very place where the shell landed. This drawing is very important for us. As you can see, this was the line of fire. This was the place of impact. And according to the results of the investigation, the line of fire was 176 degrees and 29.76. This is to the south-east, which is important to know. This is another sketch, and what is interesting is that this material originated from the Muslim army. It depicts the angle between the surface and the shell. As you can see, it says that the angle was 70 degrees. This is a copy of a map, and this is my idea that I will explain on the flip chart. According to the material that I have, I believe that the experts who participated in the investigation were professionals. In keeping with this official report and the documentation, we have this image of Sarajevo. The green line represents the line of confrontation. These are the two buildings and the place of impact. According to the documentation, the direction of fire was at 176 degrees. That was the angle. And that poses another interesting question, which is why is it that within the UN we have two different sets of documents, two different reports and two different conclusions about the single investigation. In the other set of documentation another angle of descent is mentioned. As far as the first angle of descent is concerned, 176 degrees, we know what was used there and that was a 120-millimetre grenade or shell. The same ordnance used to be used in the Soviet Union. I know the weapon very well, since I'm a professional soldier. This booklet represents the system description and data on the weapons system and according to it we can see that there are six different standards of that particular weapons system. Taking that the degree was 70 degrees and that this was the line of fire after comparing that against the standards, we can conclude the following: From this area, which is 900 metres, and then the next area is 1400 metres, the next area from which such a projectile could have been fired is 2.000 metres, which is at the very line of separation. Theatrically speaking, it could have been launched from the Serbian side. The following three possibilities for firing were at 3.700 metres, 3.400 metres and 3.600 metres. I visited the location today with my own expert group. We were here, and here, and here, and I have no doubt in my mind that this place was unacceptable, that no shell could have come from here. There's no possibility to fire a shell from this position at the place where it actually landed. Now I'm talking about the terrain where the Serbian troops are. I am a soldier, a colonel, and this is indeed something that has to be done within the framework of a special investigation requiring experts, prosecutors, and perhaps members of a military court. However, it is necessary for us only to realise that this was wrong. As for the other direction, this was the distance between the place of firing and the place of impact, which is 2400 metres. I was there today and there's absolutely no possibility to fire a shell from this area. There are slopes there and forest and there's no possibility to fire from there. I photographed the area, and I will have the photographs ready, showing all of these places. I can also show you a map with the exact data and directions. The main issue with the official experts was that they only tested the angles and directions, automatically blaming the Serbs. However, I believe it is incorrect and that it requires a more thorough investigation followed by a complete ballistics test, trying to decide on all positions from which there could have been firing as well as comparing those against the places where artillery batteries are located. Again, I want to say that the results are wrong, that the documentation used is wrong, and that the conclusion is absolutely incorrect. The consequences of this event and its investigation are yet to be felt. Yesterday we saw aerial attacks, resulting in civilian casualties. I believe it is absolutely unacceptable, especially for me as a professional soldier who cannot agree with the situation in which we follow a powerful, influential group without the possibility to explain our own position, such as the one we have. To repeat, I'm a citizen of my country, and, as such, have I to say the following. Let us stop accusing falsely. Let us stop the hatred towards the Serb side. I don't want to talk about the Muslim-held areas. I don't want to accuse anyone. This is an issue to be resolved by professionals, experts. What is necessary for us, however, it is necessary to carry out a thorough investigation with all of the details and arguments to be included."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
