utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to suggest, since we have all had the patience to listen to this, to admit the video footage and the transcript that accompanies it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, anything on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have no objection. Just a brief way of explanation, when we realised that Colonel Demurenko is indeed coming to testify, we realised that he actually made this presentation before TV stations and we asked the Bosnian government I believe to deliver the tape, which we received a few days ago. So that's the way we -- we got it, and we obviously immediately gave it to the Defence. It is a contemporaneous report and we believe it should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Colonel, can I just ask for one little bit clarification. You said, I think, several times during your interview in the footage that it would have been impossible for anyone to fire a mortar grenade from those areas depicted on or indicated on your line going down 176 degrees. Because you said that there were hills and forests, I believe, and it would be impossible to fire a mortar grenade from anywhere in that area. That's how I understood it. But I'm not sure I understand why would it be impossible. A mortar grenade, I suppose, can be fired from many places and -- and if there's a clearance in the woods or if there's a road, then you can probably fire it from there. So what supported your conclusion that it would have been impossible to fire a mortar from anywhere in that area? Just explain to us very briefly. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you excuse me for my poor English, I will try to do it very shortly by -- on the paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's try to get the mics near to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 120-millimetres mortar is very specific, very old type of weapon. Really this is a tape and tube. No special equipment for very, very specific point for firing. And as you know maybe, we have this type of weapon, only six charges. It's an a specific small back with explosion. The principle of the firing for a mortar, this is a tape, this is a tube, and we can to change of this angle only on the vertical, not on horizontal and six charges. And therefore, during the maximum horizontal, for example, 89 degrees and -- like this, and one charges, the maximum parabola, if we will have this angle as a minimum, for example, 30, 30 degrees, and the six charges of this, if this is a parabola but a little bit other, like this. And in Sarajevo, in this incident, it was absolutely clear that this is the two building, this is the crater, this is the terrain. This is boundary, confrontation line, this is BiH. This is the Serbian. Both sides. And we know exactly, in accordance with data of expert, I don't know -- approximately 60, 70 degrees, maybe 70, I forget it, but all the same now. And in this case, I mean this angle, this angle has therefore only one, two, three, four, five, six, point for firing position, and we inspected each -- I mean on Serbian side, even on confrontation line each position with photoparat. In three of these firing positions, it was stones. It's not road, it's stones. Absolutely impossible to stay plate on the stones. In accordance with military point of view, absolutely impossible. And one position is the forest, the mine can't move through there, the part of the trees, because blast immediately. Therefore, we check it on the photoparat photo, each four positions, and five position with other angle. Do you remember from this point? No inspection of the BiH. We said, okay, maybe could be next step for us, but absolutely clear 100 per cent that Serbs can't to organise the provided shelling from this position according with this angle. Angle is no without doubts, because expert, ballistic expert. That's all. Is it clear, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Colonel, would there not be quite a large margin around each of these six firing points? And even so, the further out you get, the larger the margin within which the fire could have been shot is increased? So if you take the example with the six charges, that -- I mean, if it was fired from there, it could have been fire, I suppose, quite a large area. It did not necessarily have to be fired from the position where you were and you took the photograph. If, for instance, a couple of hundred metres away there would have been a road or something else, the shot could have come from there. So are you able really to exclude that the mortar could not have been fired even from an area adjacent to the place where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to emphasise one thing once again. I know this weapon very, very well. Maybe my -- maybe the interpretation of the word "charge" was misleading. There are no different shells, six shells there. There are six charges. And it's charged manually. You put the shell inside the tube and it flies up. So the firing tables for mortars that you saw in that video footage show that in that direction only six charges are possible, either one, two, three, all the six were taken into account. Margins of deviation are measured in metres, like ten to 15 metres, the size of this room, but the margin of deviation cannot be 100 metres. We took into account ballistic trajectories. It's the science of physics. We cannot go beyond that. If you take a certain line of fire, only six possible firing points exist, depending on the charges used. We photographed an area of 20, 30 square metres. We always proceeded from a certain surface on which the mortar had to rely. It cannot hang in the air. It cannot be suspended on a tree. We showed the photographs and we saw the ground was pure, clear. No mortar had stood there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thanks to Mr. Harhoff, Judge Harhoff, sorry, the witness has already clarified certain points, but I do have a few more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, since I have shown you that document that General Janvier addressed to Kofi Annan on the 28th of August, the day of the incident, and you read the passage that said it was very difficult, in fact impossible to determine with accuracy the origin of fire, because it is impossible to determine the charge used in the projectile. If we do not know the charge and the angle of fire, is there anyone who can make a real conclusion as opposed to an assumption, and is this consistent with your view?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, in the report by General Janvier to the United Nations addressed personally to Secretary-General Kofi Annan, you've read it just a moment ago, it said it is very difficult to determine the origin of fire because it was impossible to determine the charge used. That's what the report said. Is this somehow related to what you testified today?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us something about those reports, those other reports that you only saw when you came here to testify, reports dated the 28th and 29th. Are the bearings alone sufficient to make any conclusions beyond a reasonable doubt?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: It would be sufficient in order to say what didn't happen in my report and say, in fact, did say what didn't happen. But in order to determine what happened, it was necessary to continue the investigation, to form a team that would inquire to the full and find the perpetrator. But I don't know that it ever happened. The shelling continued and the investigation went nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you one more sketch that was admitted into evidence through another witness that I'm not going to mention, and I would like you to look at that drawing, that sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P632.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, you have already marked on your own drawing those two rectangles for buildings. I have to ask you, as a layman, if a target was located between two such buildings, would it be possible -- how shall I put this? Maybe the Chamber will not allow me to ask this directly, but would it be able -- would it be possible to aim at an invisible target under those circumstances and, as we know, you were on the spot.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Generally speaking, mortars were specially designed to target aims behind obstacles, around a corner, over and above a building, and they have their particular peculiar ballistic trajectory. However, the chances that the first shell would really hit a narrow street are one in a million. Of course it happens, but it's really one in a million. If you fired one million shells, then one of them would land in such a small narrow street.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you one more thing. On this sketch, on this chart, does it faithfully reflect the site of the crater that you went to inspect that day?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Well, this is an approximate, a rough sketch. It is not done to scale. But basically it is a faithful reflection of that alley, the buildings on both sides, the distance between them, around 15 metres. There is one proviso. On this drawing I see a trace of a shell impact on one building and something I cannot identify on top of the other building. I cannot confirm this because I never saw anything like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know this is a trace of a mortar shell, this circle? I admit we have discussed this and I have to admit before the Chamber that we did discuss this sketch. I showed it to the witness. I asked the witness this precise question . But, Witness, what do you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: If I'm answering the question why do you think this is a trace made by a mortar shell, if you remember that drawing of the angle of descent, the officer investigating the incident had part of a tail-fin in his hands, part of a tail-fin of that alleged shell, and it was said on the basis of that that it was 120-millimetre shell. But I personally never saw it. So it was one-third of that shell, so the other two-thirds must have been fragmented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I actually want to ask you this. When you were there at the site, did you observe anything peculiar expect for the crater? Did you see anything fresh, any fresh traces that could have been a result of an event which take place on that day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Don't answer the question. Let us hear Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's leading. The proper question would be what did you see when you were there at any given time, can you describe. What does "fresh" mean in this context?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, he could ask did you see any traces. Did you see any traces? Don't shake your head. Answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no new traces. I didn't see anything unusual. Unusual for me, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Expect for the crater on the ground, which you inspected. Witness, just tell me, please. Answer my question. Expect for that crater that was there at the site; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Except for that crater and another four craters of the alleged additional four shells landing from different directions. We inspected all of them and there was quite a lot of doubt as to how those craters are to be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you hear what I read out to you from the second report on the 29th? When did you hear about the fact that there was no audible trace? Nobody registered audibly the trajectory of the shell, nor was it registered on any radars. When did you hear of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't think the witness has mentioned radars yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is so, Mr. Tapuskovic. Reformulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can only go back to what I put to the witness when I read it out from the report of the 29th, where it is stated that there had been a report of UN Military Observers who neither heard nor saw any shells fired from the territory of the -- territory under the control of the RS army. When did the witness hear of this? I already put this to the witness. I need now to know when he heard of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The complaint is that you have mentioned radars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, I'm a little bit tired, yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, did you learn at the time of any other report, in addition to those two that ended on your desk based on which you undertook certain measures. Did you, in the following days, learn anything else about the event which took place on the 28th and what significance did it have for your reasoning about this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm now being asked to comment on two or three documents which were a result of that investigation, whereas at the time I had ten, 15, 20 various sources of information. Some of them were reports of UNMOs. Some of them were reports produced by observation posts of the UN. Some were reports produced by civilian police. In addition to these, there were also verbal accounts of residents. I wouldn't want to comment on each of those sources right now, especially since I don't have them in writing right now. But at any rate, all of these documents, all of these sources were heterogeneous. They pointed to different directions based on which I concluded that one should not jump to conclusions. One needed to make a diligent investigation before coming up with any results and pointing fingers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You said you had 10, 15, 20 various sources of information and all of them different. Is that so? But you don't have them here. Are they obtainable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some of them should certainly be in UNPROFOR archives. I told you that we had various sources of information. We had reports of Military Observers, we had reports of observation posts within the UN, plus we had civilian police reports. All of these documents should exist in UN archives or UNPROFOR archives. In addition to this, we also had accounts of civilians. I don't think that I need to elaborate on these right now, but if you want me to, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just concentrate on one point. You say that they were all different. Different in what respects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None of these sources identified accurately the source or the origin of fire. Some sources indicated the following: We didn't hear this. The observation post stated this, that we didn't register on our monitors any shells in the air. Some of them said that there was no audible record of a shell flying through the air. Third sources stated that there were no five explosions but just one, where some sources indicated that there were five shells. So all of these sources pointed to various explanations and directions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We should take the break now. I believe you will be with us for some time, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Since you have ruled on the video being admitted as well as the transcript, I just wanted to remind you that no number was assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let a number be given to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the video interview and the corresponding transcript DD00-4130 will become Exhibit D286.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And another thing, Your Honours, the sketch the witness made was in response to Judge Harhoff's question. I would like to tender it as a Defence exhibit unless you decide otherwise, as something that was done on the request from -- upon the request from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it may be exhibited, but I just wonder whether it is sufficiently intelligible, without markings to indicate what is what. I don't know. Judge Harhoff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, if I'm held responsible for the production of this evidence, I think I can interpret it fairly well, but we might wish to ask the witness to just indicate with a pen the explosion to the right on the lower part. If you just put an X. And then-- then starting from the left, you say charge six, C-6 and 5 and 4 and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. And you put "Charlie" in front of it so we know that it's the charges. C-6, C-5, C-4, C, the letter C.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the hard copy sketch will be admitted as D287.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, we spent a great deal of time on your testimony so far. And I will try to conclude my examination-in-chief with a few additional questions. First, I'd like to ask you to tell us something about whether after you had given the interview, and you have explained circumstances and your reasons, in the days that followed after the interview was broadcast, did you have any problems?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges whether after the interview you had some difficulties, problems, unpleasantness. Perhaps you can explain.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I can. My difficulty was actually quite simple, to remain alive. Because literally on the following day, Captain Salajdzic, liaison officer between the BH command and Sector Sarajevo, came to me and told me, "You have one day of life to live, Colonel. You have no chance of leaving the headquarters. At any intersection, you can be killed. An order was issued to kill you." This is what I was told by the BH officer. As for UNPROFOR, initially there was a decision taken by the commander to send me away, within 24 hours to send me away. In reality, it was not a terrible problem for me, because I wasn't afraid of going back to my homeland. However, the UNPROFOR commander for Bosnia-Herzegovina was smart enough to listen to other voices there, who told him if we send Demurenko away we will acknowledge publicly that we are afraid of the truth and that we do not want the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yeah. This requires a little more explanation, Witness. Remind us now who was this person who told you that you have only one day to live. You said he was a captain. Who was-- Captain what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His rank was that of a Captain. His last name was a Salajdzic. He was a nephew of the BH prime minister and he was a liaison officer between the BH army and Sector Sarajevo. He was with my -- he came to my headquarters on a daily basis. I apologise for switching into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But did he offer any further explain as to why you only had one day to live? Did he explain how this would come about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In quite a detailed way. He said that on that occasion I took a pro-Serb and anti-Bosnian position, which wasn't true, but that was their interpretation. This made certain commanders and certain structures in Bosnia angry. I'm not sure quite who they were, but automatically I was listed as enemy, and enemies are usually destroyed in wartime. As for the means that they were going to implement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who -- did he say -- did he identify the persons or the entity that would be responsible for killing you or that will kill you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally he didn't say who had taken that sort of a decision, but he said quite clearly the following: He knew that I crossed the confrontation line several times every day. I went through a Bosnian check-point, through a Serbian and then again through a Bosnian, through a Serbian check-point, any time I went through a Bosnian check-point, and I was travelling in a car which wasn't armoured, it was very easy to shoot me through. He explained that in detailed way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Just answer the questions I'm asking. Don't volunteer anything. Did you find his report credible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried not to believe him. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you report this to any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did go to a church after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you report this to anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but I went to a church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You never made a report to any of your army officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm an officer. I'm not afraid of anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You just went to a church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what? You prayed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I begged the All Mighty to help me stay alive for the sake of my family. I believe that he heard my pleas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, a little while ago you mentioned some indicia to the Judges. What sort of indications were you talking about? I probably would not have asked you this had you not mentioned this in one of your answers. I don't know on whose question that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I apologise, indicators of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, I think you mentioned some indicators, although I might be wrong, but some indicators about a terrorist activity when you were asked about your opinion on where the shell had come from.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes. After all, I'm not a specialist on anti-terrorist activities. Rather, I'm a specialist on peace keeping operations. But nevertheless, there was something that pointed to the fact that this was not a shelling incident but, rather, an explosion caused by terrorists inside the city. I will list the indicators, starting with the most important ones. First that certain facts were not consistent. One shell killed 120 people, whereas four other shells only wounded three or four people. Therefore, it is illogical, how come one shell was that effective, in quotation marks, and how come other shells were so ineffective. That was the first point. The second point: On two occasions within two years in 1994 and in 1995, at the same place, in a market frequented by so many people in a small street in a market called Markale, there were explosions that killed numerous people, peaceful residents. It is simply improbable that on each occasion a shell would be fired from the mountainous area and land in the very same spot killing so many people on two occasions. Third point, if an expert proved that he found a crater and a portion of the shell, that means that only the other part of the shell was fragmented. I know exactly what a shell does. It is made out of iron. It has no -- it has no clusters. And it is simply improbable that a shell, being what it is, ended up killing with its fragments over 100 people. It was not made up of little clusters. Plus there was some other indicators. There was no audible trace. It wasn't registered on any radars or anything of the sort. So all of these facts point to the conclusion that this was a planned operation, a provocative act that gave somebody material to blame the Serbs. I want to assure that you I'm a very objective person. It is not my aim here to defend the Serbs. All I'll say is that they should not be satanised. It is quite wrong to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What about the crater?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's very easy, believe me. After the war, I discussed this with specialists in anti-terrorist combat. You take an urn, like for garbage, you put a detonation device and take the explosive device, you push the shell downwards and you create the impression of a -- the same as when a shell explodes. On the one hand it is a very hand-fisted imitation but on the other hand it has a certain amount of sophistication. It's an improvisation. I cannot say that I have evidence for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't want to take Mr. Tapuskovic's time, but we have had evidence here to show or to tell us that a mortar could not explode just by being dropped from a couple of metres. It would need to have much more velocity in order to actually explode. So how would you make the mortar grenade explode from a very short distance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Moreover, I know how to -- how these bearings, how the clusters work. A shell can explode only by being fired from a mortar. If you throw it from a rooftop, it won't explode. That's true. But I'm saying again, to simulate an explosion of a shell using a different explosive device is not difficult, because the crater is the same. If you take a shell and fix it using screws or whatever else and explode it with a different detonator, the crater will look the same. There are factors that make me believe that it couldn't have been a mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The information that you gave in answer to Mr. Tapuskovic was a response to his question as to what did you say, what are you saying are the indicators of a terrorist attack. Are you saying that the three pieces of information that you just gave us are indicative of a terrorist attack? Because that's not clear to me. It's not clear to me whether that is what you are saying. And if that is so, then -- then why are they so indicative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not a high-flying specialist in legal matters or anti-terrorist combat and I cannot determine what is an anti-terrorist act -- what is a terrorist act and what isn't, but I'm 100 per cent sure and I try to convince you of the first part of my testimony which has to do with facts. The second part are my own conclusions about what could have been done and how. It is not my task here to convince that you it was a terrorist act and I was not prepared for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, one question remains. The issue of fragments. If the incident was in fact a terrorist attack and not a mortar shell, what about the fragments that were found? You said at one stage that they could have been put there, but looking at the facts, do you think you're right? If those shell fragments were put there, were attached, don't you think that the people who were at the market could have noticed that? Do you think that people at the market would have accepted to be sacrificed like sheep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is obvious. It is a real crime, whoever may have perpetrated it. And of course, those were people who were dreaming of staying alive, having their families, having their life continue. They did not think of death. They never wanted to be sacrificed. As for the shrapnel found in the bodies of those dead and wounded, part of those did not belong to the iron part of the shell, but that in itself does not mean that this shell did not have an additional charge, because in every impact, fragments of glass and other objects find their way into people's bodies. If it was indeed an act of agent provocateur, I think that we cannot find evidence of it 12 years later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my examination-in-chief. I would like to thank the witness and you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have concluded, Mr. Tapuskovic? Yes. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, we have about a little bit more than half an hour left today, and I take it it will be -- also take much of tomorrow, although of course, I'm in the Trial Chamber's hands, but I intend to use as much time as I need. I understand that you had plans to travel away, so I just want to say that, and I don't think it is realistic to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have been informed that the witness will be available tomorrow. Mr. Tapuskovic to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm that he will be here until 11.00. I don't know what your ruling will be. We are starting at 8.00 a.m. and his plane is not before 1.00 p.m. So if my learned friend took as much time as I did, and I really overdid it, then I don't know how far that would take us. Maybe 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's start with some background information you gave us in the beginning of your testimony. In 1992 to 1994 you were not stationed in Sarajevo. You were not in Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think the second microphone needs to be turned on as well.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was not in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So the first time you came to Bosnia was in fact in -- I think you said in the first few days in January 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Then you explained us your career in -- in the Soviet army, the Russian Federation army. You said you were a commander of a platoon, a company, a battalion, a regiment. What kind of formations were that, artillery, infantry, mechanised?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: All of them or were you focussing on -- I don't think you first command an infantry platoon and then an artillery regiment. Which units did you command?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I can answer this. The Soviet as well as the Russian system of education is different from the western system in a way, and I can-- I know something about this because I had training in America. On the tactical level, a Moscow institution prepares, trains officers from platoon commanders up to battalion commanders. So everything that is at the disposal of the platoon, company, and battalion, we had to learn about. In a mechanised infantry battalion, we have a 120-millimetre battery. I know that very well. At the next level --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. But what kind of battalion did you command, an infantry? Actual command not learning about it, just commanding. Was it an infantry or a tank or an artillery battalion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: In Russian, yes, we call it motorised rifle battalion, and that includes mortar battery, mortar unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that would be an infantry unit rather than a mechanised unit?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Mechanised, motorised. Not mortar. It involves either infantry or APC-equipped. That would be mechanised in western terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In fact I was forced in earlier times of my career to learn a lot about the Soviet army. So I can probably tell, but I've never thought about that from that experience. Anyway, the regiment that you commanded, again what was that? Was it artillery, was it motorised, was it mechanised?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: It was mechanised regiment, including three battalions, also mechanised, in western terminology, an artillery unit, a rocket unit, a tank unit and 12 different companies, all in all, 2.000 troops, privates, Sergeants, that is, it NCOs and officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And for how long did you command that regiment?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Two and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you have a Chief of Staff there as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes. I was Chief of Staff of that regiment before becoming its commander, and in my further career I remained commander in the Far East.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And is that helpful being a Chief of Staff of a unit before becoming its commander?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: It is a standard hierarchy, a standard step on that ladder. I was Chief of Staff of battalion first, before becoming commander of the battalion, and then I was Chief of Staff of the regiment before becoming commander of that regiment. It is an absolutely standard way of promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it makes sense, does it not, because the Chief of Staff is really the second most knowledgeable officer in any unit. He is the alter ego of the commander.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think you also told us that as a Chief of Staff you basically have the same duties as the commander. You also have, you know, the authority to order and so on, just basically being the stand-in to the commander.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I don't know whether you have much information about the Yugoslav system. You talked a little bit about the weaponry that was basically very, very similar or identical. Would the same apply to the functions of the Chief of Staff and the commander? What you just said about the Soviet army about the role of the Chief of Staff, the relationship to the commander, that would also apply to the VRS as you saw it working in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I'm not prepared to say with 100 per cent certainty that the powers and authority are the same, the system is the same, but there is a 70 per cent similarity. I believe the Yugoslav army was in a way a copy of the Soviet army. Yugoslav officers attended Soviet army schools at the highest level, and I believe that in all armies of the Warsaw Pact countries, the Chief of Staff had basically the same position as in -- in other member countries. In Sarajevo Sector, I practically had no dealings with the leadership of either warring parties. And that supported my duty of impartiality. I only had to have contact with liaison officers, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Because your main function as a Chief of Staff was to organise the inner workings of the UNPROFOR staff, which was comprised of many nations? Was that your prime function as a Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR, Sector Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Generally speaking, the primary task of any Chief of Staff is to maintain combat readiness of subordinate troops, their preparedness to efficiently operate. That was tactical operation, intelligence, although the word "intelligence" wasn't used. In Yugoslavia it was called collection of information, cooperation with your own units and neighbouring units, and only then did the Chief of Staff have to perform as a stand-in for the commander in command functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. What I'm trying to get is the UNPROFOR solution, in terms of the division of labour between the commander, the Chief of Staff and perhaps deputies was slightly different, because in UNPROFOR, in at least in 1995 there was a commander, there was a Chief of Staff, but there was also deputy commanders, and one deputy commander would have been a French colonel, Colonel Meille. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Colonel, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when the commander, you mentioned a General Bachelet, was away, then the deputy commander -- I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if I can continue, if General Bachelet or his predecessor Gobillard was away, there was a custom that Colonel Meille would be the acting commander. Did you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Not quite. First of all, Colonel Meille arrived much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can we go briefly into the private session, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think, Colonel, you wanted to explain something about the acting commander.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Colonel, I believe you wanted to mention something about the acting commander, Colonel Meille. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: In any army there is hierarchy of substitutes, the first substitute is usually the Chief of Staff and then the second substitute is responsible for combat readiness, as a rule. In this case, in our sector we followed the standard procedure with the exception that Colonel Meille was only there for six months out of the year that I was there. He came in May and left in September. We knew each well. He was my close associate, and his job was to cooperate with and supervise the French contingent, which would have been difficult for me since I don't speak French. Since 50 or 60 per cent of our total troops were the French Battalion, commander when he had to go away, left as his deputy the French commander, not the Russian commander, logically. But I cannot remember a single occasion when General Bachelet would have been absent and I did not cooperate closely with my French colleague. We were constantly in contact and cooperated on all issues. On the 20th of August, General Bachelet was there -- sorry, on the 28th of August, General Bachelet was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me very, very briefly address the Russian Battalion, because you mentioned two aspects of it. First of all, you talk about the extremely unfavourable location of the Russian Battalion. But there was a couple of very good observation points. For instance, one of them was at a restaurant called Vidikovac. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I seem to remember that was in the south-east.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, south-west, interpreter's --

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: From that vantage point you can see the entire valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this area was controlled by -- apart from the Russian Battalion who was there, was controlled by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the part where Vidikovac was located?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Partly, yes. But if you don't mind, that doesn't mean that the positions of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were equally advantageous, tactically speaking, as the observation post of the Russian Battalion, and the reason is simple. UNPROFOR located their observation posts wherever that they pleased. Whereas the warring parties could put up their observation posts only where it was possible. The other party often got there before them. As soon as one location was free, the other party would occupy it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But Vidikovac, being the top of Trebevic mountain, was within the part controlled by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes. That was a routine practice among the military. This is where the observation post is known as an observation location, because you want to take up the most favourable location for observing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Because I just wanted to make the point that having occasionally not very good positions for weaponry does not mean that you could not have good observation points and then link those two elements, the weaponry on one side, and the observation points on another side. That is a common military -- military tactic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I apologise. What exactly this has to do with the observation post of the Russian Battalion, what does this have to do with the weaponry location? Are you referring to the SRK location? You know, what link is there between UNPROFOR as a peace keeping force and one of the warring sides? Russian Battalion did not fight on the side of the SRK, or perhaps I misinterpreted your words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, maybe I wasn't clear enough. I just putting to you that normally if you have some weaponry which is not in a very good location, if you combine it with a observation point, I'm talking about military in general, not about the warring capacities of the Russian Battalion. So if you combine weaponry and great observation, that's a way to conduct military business, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: In abstract terms, without referring to the Serbs or to the Russians, in that case, you are correct. But only in one case if this is -- you are not referring to guided missiles, but, rather, to Howitzers, mortars, and so on. Observation is of no use to you if you are using a tank, infantry weapons or anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I agree. And I was also talking about the ABiH. I was talking any military force in that region when I was asking about the combination between weaponry on one side an observation on the other side. Let me go on to a very brief point. Also you were asked about the area of responsibility of your sector. Was the enclave of Zepa also a part of your sector?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No. Srebrenica and Zepa did not make part of your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So if General -- one of the commanders would have said that some of the enclaves, including Zepa, were part of it, you would deny that or you just don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Certainly not. An order is an order. And if a general who was my direct superior gave such an order, then naturally I would proceed with implementation of that order, especially since everybody else knew that those enclaves were the fragile points of that -- of that war, that needed special attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. You were shown a map, the UNPROFOR map which had the confrontation lines in yellow and red. Do you remember that? And you were asked who controlled the inside of that ring, and you answered it was the ABiH, and it's the SRK, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that controlled the outside of the ring. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes. Outside of Sarajevo, it was the SRK -- outside of those lines, it was the SRK, and within those lines it was the 1st Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Incidentally, did you ever meet the commander of the 1st Corps of the Muslim army, or the Bosniak army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No. I had no meetings with the corps commander. On one occasion I met the brigade commander. We had an issue to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You also talked about the civilians inside the confrontation lines and I believe you used the word "anxiousness," and you gave an example that you saw the civilians not collecting their garbage, so UNPROFOR had to take over and do that job. Is one -- would you call that a lethargic attitude towards life in general?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite an appropriate word to describe the situation. Especially in winter time, when people are hibernating. I was quite surprised by this. Prior to that, I had experience of fierce fighting in the former Soviet Union territory. And I was all ready for war when I arrived in Sarajevo, and upon arriving there, I started asking, well, where is the war? I mean, there was just occasional exchange of fire and most often by drunk soldiers firing into the sky, tracer bullets and so on. And I also saw a lot of love couples walking in the street, so I was quite surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And would you describe those -- or would you accept that the lethargic attitude of people is a explanation perhaps that the civilians were under siege for two, three years already, that they kind of lost almost their will to -- to lead a normal life, as it were?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Naturally, that is one of the explanations. The other one is that the best, most energetic and just plainly speaking different people had already left the area. Some of them had left the area entirely, some of them went to fight on, say, the side of the BH army and so on. So the least active segment of the population remained in town, so what you said makes sense, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I said that I wanted to discuss two brief aspects of the Russian Battalion. We discussed one. The second one is this small incident about the Russian Battalion which needed to be taken out by you. And did you remember, was it the case that the unfortunate Russian soldiers were caught on Debelo Brdo between the French who also had an observation point there, and just between a battle between the Serbs and the ABiH and so the help of UNPROFOR the Russian soldiers had to be taken away. Is that a fair characterisation of the way the situation evolved?

utterances.speaker: ANDREI DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I think that we're discussing the same incident. If I can remember, it was in late July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I want to raise a matter with the witness. Witness, you remember that in your examination-in-chief you indicated that there were some 10 or 15 or 20 reports about the explosion, all with different results. I believe you said some of them might be with UNPROFOR. One, were these reports that you actually saw and read? Just yes or no. Were these reports that you actually saw and read? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I read several contradictory reports of UNPROFOR, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: About how many? About how many? Can you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read six, seven, or eight such reports. When I mentioned the figure of 15 to 20, I also said that some of them were verbal, oral which were not written down. And, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The six, seven, or eight that were written, where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Where did they come from, where did they emanate from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In UNPROFOR there were several sections that were duty-bound to report. I will list those sections to you. First of all, there was a report coming from the operations centre, collecting information from all forces. Then there was a report of G2 section which was an intelligence military section. Then there was a military police section. Then there was a report of Military Observers, that was the fourth report. Then there were various reports coming from individual battalions, say the Russian Battalion commander and so on. So I can go on listing these reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... In the Prosecution case, how many reports did you submit on this incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I also thought about that during the last break. We had the G2 report, we had the Bosnian, local Bosnian police report which the witness has in his hands as well. We had the report of the French engineers. I think the witness showed it into the cameras. We had our own expert, Mr. Higgs. Of course that was not available to the witness. And I think there was another report by a Colonel Powers from the US, a very short one, which also addresses these issues. But all these reports kind of aren't reports that are original. They refer to each other and kind of summarise. So it is probably very difficult to say how many reports you have which are of original nature. And then, of course, you have the UNMO reports. The two we have seen from patrol leader Konings. You can call them reports, although they are more observations. And, yes, Mr. Knustad and other people of course as the witness pointed out made oral reports as to what they heard but I would say that there are four main reports which the Prosecution has submitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you just heard the reports that were offered in the Prosecution's case. Are you in a position to say whether any of the reports that you saw and read was not included in the list just outlined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listed by me? Named by me or by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, named by the Prosecutor. I'm trying to see whether any of the reports that you said you saw and you read we have not yet seen. Because I want to see them. I want to make that clear. I'd like to see the reports which you say all indicated different results, different conclusions, and so my first -- my first effort is to see whether we have them here already or how many of them we have. So I'm asking whether, having heard what the Prosecutor said he produced in his case, whether you saw any other reports, saw and read any other report on this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood the question. Naturally I'm not -- I don't know Mr. Higgs. Perhaps I did read his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, briefly on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just a report by Mr. Higgs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want a long speech. It's late in the evening. Yes, now go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to be of assistance to you and everybody else. I picked three or four documents out of all of the documents, but there are many other reports that were already admitted, say, Baxter report, Powers report. There's a whole number of reports by intelligence services. I only used the official reports, which were introduced through some other witnesses into evidence. I thought that what I used here was not sufficient. We need to use other material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going conclude the day's proceedings, and tomorrow I will return to this matter. We begin at 8.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 6th day of July, 2007, at 8.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.,
